evidence.claim: Country roads link working farms, cypress water and a Seminole battlefield
evidence.quote: The Scenic Sumter Heritage Byway traverses pastoral farmlands, cattle ranches, and horse farms, featuring lush open fields alongside quiet country towns, hardwood forests, the tranquil Withlacoochee River lined with moss-covered cypress trees

evidence.claim: Country roads link working farms, cypress water and a Seminole battlefield
evidence.quote: Points of interest along the route include the Dade Battlefield State Historic Site

evidence.claim: The Scenic Sumter Heritage Byway runs 62 miles through working farms, ranches, forests and waterways in Sumter County.
evidence.quote: Florida Scenic Highway 62 Miles Through the Heart of Sumter County The Scenic Sumter Heritage Byway winds through rural communities, working farms and ranches, historic sites, forests, waterways

evidence.claim: Open fields give way to hardwood forest, with moss-covered cypress along the Withlacoochee River and Lake Panasoffkee among the route’s water landmarks.
evidence.quote: featuring lush open fields alongside quiet country towns, hardwood forests, the tranquil Withlacoochee River lined with moss-covered cypress trees, and the beautiful Lake Panasoffkee.

evidence.claim: Designated a Florida Scenic Highway in 2013, the corridor was created to preserve and share the area’s natural, recreational and historic resources.
evidence.quote: Designated a Florida Scenic Highway in 2013, the 62-mile route was created to help preserve and share the natural, recreational and historic resources

evidence.claim: The campaign brought together the county chamber of commerce, Webster and Bushnell, county government, businesses, veterans’ groups and residents.
evidence.quote: The Sumter County Chamber of Commerce, the cities of Webster and Bushnell, the Sumter County government, businesses, community leaders, veterans’ groups, and individuals worked to have 62 miles of road in Sumter County designated

evidence.claim: The route entered the state program as a candidate in 2010; after designation, supporters gathered at Dade Battlefield in January 2014 to cut the ribbon.
evidence.quote: On September 1, 2010, the Scenic Sumter Heritage Byway was designated a candidate for the Florida Scenic Highway Program.

evidence.claim: The battlefield was one of the historic places included along the new byway.
evidence.quote: Points of interest along the route include the Dade Battlefield State Historic Site

evidence.quote: CR 470: runs east and west from SR 44 near the Sumter-Citrus County Line along the west side of Lake Panasoffkee, then briefly joins US 301 in Sumterville

evidence.claim: Black Seminoles settled near Boggy Island at Lake Panasoffkee around 1813, naming their settlement Sitarkey’s Village after an Alachua Seminole who had settled there.
evidence.quote: Black Seminoles settled near the Boggy Island area of Lake Panasoffkee around 1813 and named it Sitarkey's Village after Sitarkey, an Alachua Seminole who had settled in the area.

evidence.claim: They raised corn, rice and sugar cane, along with cattle, horses and hogs.
evidence.quote: The black Seminoles raised corn, rice, and sugar cane, which Horatio Dexter, one of the first settlers in the area, gave them in 1822.  In addition, residents in Sitarkey's Village raised livestock, including cattle, horses, and hogs.

evidence.claim: During the Second Seminole War, families used the area as a refuge.
evidence.quote: Generally, the Sitakey's Village area was untouched during the Second Seminole War, allowing black Seminole families to use the area as a refuge from the war.

evidence.claim: After the battle of Wahoo Swamp, Osceola moved to Panasoffkee Swamp to live with Black Seminoles.
evidence.quote: After the battle of Wahoo Swamp, Osceola, possibly suffering from the effects of malaria that he contracted during the Seminole occupation of Fort Drane moved to the Panasoffkee Swamp to live with the black Seminoles

evidence.claim: General Thomas Sidney Jesup raided the village in January 1837, capturing 16 Black Seminoles while others escaped.
evidence.quote: On January 10, 1837, General Thomas Sidney Jesup, looking for Osceola, raided the village. Osceola and three warriors fled. Jesup captured 16 black Seminoles while the rest of the village escaped.

evidence.claim: A military road ran through the ground now preserved at Dade Battlefield.
evidence.quote: In 1828, soldiers and slaves constructed the Fort King Road

evidence.claim: Soldiers and enslaved people cut the Fort King Road through pines and understory in 1828, making a passage 20 feet wide.
evidence.quote: In 1828, soldiers and slaves constructed the Fort King Road by cutting the understory and pine trees, leaving a 20-foot (6.1-meter) wide road.

evidence.claim: On December 28, 1835, Seminole warriors and Black Seminole allies fought Major Francis L. Dade’s soldiers here.
evidence.quote: it preserves the Second Seminole War battlefield where tribal Seminole warriors and Black Seminole allies fought soldiers under the command of Major Francis L. Dade on December 28, 1835.

evidence.claim: The United States was attempting to force the Seminoles from Florida to Indian Territory.
evidence.quote: the U.S. was attempting to force the Seminoles to move away from their land in Florida provided by the Treaty of Moultrie Creek (following the American annexation of Spanish Florida see the Adams-Onis Treaty) and relocate to Indian Territory

evidence.claim: The battle began the Second Seminole War.
evidence.quote: The Dade battle began the Second Seminole War.

evidence.claim: The park preserves pine flatwoods and a live oak hammock; the breastworks near its museum are a replica.
evidence.quote: The 80-acre (32 ha) park includes 40 acres (160,000 m2) of pine flatwoods  and a live oak hammock.

evidence.claim: the breastworks near its museum are a replica.
evidence.quote: The museum which details the Seminole War lies 49 feet (15 meters) from the replica of the breastworks

evidence.claim: In 1925, Travelon Magazine called Sumter County the “storehouse of Florida” and described making a good living on ten acres, an agricultural ambition tied to the landscape this corridor now shares.
evidence.quote: A 1925 edition of Travelon Magazine called Sumter County the “ storehouse of Florida ” and a “ place where good living could be made on ten acres of land ”.

evidence.claim: Seminoles also held councils and Green Corn Dances in the Lake Panasoffkee area.
evidence.quote: The Seminoles used the Lake Panasoffkee area to hold councils and Green Corn Dances.

evidence.claim: The museum explains the Seminole War, while a nature trail winds through the pine flatwoods.
evidence.quote: The museum which details the Seminole War

evidence.claim: a nature trail winds through the pine flatwoods.
evidence.quote: A 3,499-foot (1,066-meter) long nature trail winds through the pine flatwoods.
